1:
The summons is heard as a legal citation. Clarke says a process is instituted against the priests, the Israelites and the house of the king, who are called on to appear and defend themselves, the accusation being that they have ensnared the people and caused them to practise idolatry. Calvin reaches the same conclusion by rejecting an alternative. Some explain the clause about judgment to mean that it is the duty of these men to do judgment and maintain government, taking the word for rectitude and a right order of things, and so read the verse as a rebuke for discharging their office badly; that sense Calvin calls too strained. The prophet is rather summoning the priests and the counsellors of the king to the tribunal of God to give an answer there, since contempt of God prevailed among the great, who were secure as though exempt from judgment and released from laws and all order. Ellicott renders the phrase more accurately as meant for you rather than toward you. Wesley states it simply, that the controversy of God is with them all.

Who the priests are is contested. Gill takes them for idolatrous priests who called themselves so and were reckoned so by others though not of the tribe of Levi, being such as Jeroboam had made or their successors, and allows that some of the family of Aaron might have continued in the cities of Israel and given in to the idolatrous worship of those times; he notes that the word signifies princes as well, and that some render it so. Henry keeps both classes: priests in holy orders, since there were cities of priests and Levites among the ten tribes who probably stayed in their own lot after the revolt and did what of their office could be done at a distance from the temple, and also those only pretending to holy orders, the priests of the calves. His interest is in the levelling. Neither the sanctity of the priesthood nor the dignity of the royal family can be expected to keep out wrath if they do not keep out sin, and it shall be no plea for the common people that they were misled by their priests and princes, since neither their meanness nor their multitude will be their exemption.

The snare and the net are located on the ground. Clarke places Mizpah beyond the Jordan in the mountains of Gilead, and Tabor as a beautiful mountain in the tribe of Zebulum, and observes that both places were eminent for hunting, whence the natural occurrence of the words snare and net in speaking of them. Ellicott makes the same geography serve a military reading: the two stand on opposite sides of the Jordan and are singled out as strongholds where the princes of the royal house, with the apostate priests, exercised their deadly hold upon the people, waylaying them as birds and beasts are snared in the mountains of prey. Wesley has the idolatry itself catching men as birds are taken in a net, and places Mizpah differently again, calling it a part of Libanus. Calvin reports and refutes a further conjecture, that the name should be taken to mean a beacon, so that the clause would run that they had been a snare instead of a beacon; the second clause about the net expanded over Tabor refutes the mistake, both being well known places.
2:
Keil and Delitzsch open on the two places named just before. Mizpah, as a parallel to Tabor, can only be the lofty Mizpah of Gilead, so that while Tabor represents the land on this side of the Jordan, Mizpah, which resembled it in situation, is chosen to represent the land to the east of the river; both were probably noted as peculiarly adapted for bird-catching, since Tabor is still thickly wooded. They add a denial the others do not make, that the supposition that these were places of sacrifice in connection with idolatrous worship cannot be inferred from the verse, nor is it rendered probable by other passages.

The phrase about being profound to make slaughter is read four ways. Gill keeps the hunting figure running: the revolters, meaning king, priests and people, formed deep laid schemes like hawkers who lay themselves flat upon the ground to manage their snares, and the slaughter is the multiplying of sacrifices offered with a great show of devotion, by which simple and unwary souls are ensnared. Clarke keeps the figure but changes the device to the deep pits which hunters make and lightly cover, so that the beasts do not discover them and fall in; and he adds a historical possibility, that as many as wished to depart from the idolatrous worship set up by Jeroboam were slaughtered. Calvin allows the usual reading of sacrifices and does not reject it, but hears contempt in the word, since to call sacrificing killing is like calling the temple the shambles; he reports a second sense the word carries, that men flatter themselves with their own counsels and think that by twining reasons together they can deceive God, but doubts whether that idea suits here and prefers the simpler meaning, that the people were so addicted to their superstitions that they could not be restored to a sound mind however often admonished. Ellicott drops the figure altogether, following Ewald and Nowack in rendering the clause that the apostates have gone deep in iniquity, and corrects the last clause to read that Jehovah is chastisement to them all, so that deceivers and deceived shall alike perish. Clarke reads that clause the same way, that as they made victims of others to their idolatry he will make victims of them to his justice, while Wesley has the revolters digging deep to hide their counsels and to slay the innocent.

On the divine knowledge the voices converge. Gill sets appearance against reality: men may cover their designs and put on a show of religion, but God, who knows all hearts, judges not according to outward appearance and cannot be deceived. Calvin turns it into a rebuke of hypocrites who defend themselves with frivolous excuses and think they thus put a restraint on God, so that he dares not urge them any more; the eyes of God are not dazzled with such fine pretences, and men are greatly deceived when they judge that celestial tribunal by their own perception. Both explain why Ephraim is named. Gill records the interpretation of Kimchi, that Ephraim means Jeroboam the son of Nebat, who was of that tribe, along with opinions that distinguish Ephraim from Israel as one tribe from nine or as ten tribes from two, though he judges it best to take both names of the ten tribes; Calvin says it was by way of honour that the name of the tribe from which the first Jeroboam sprang was given to the ten. Clarke states the verdict in eight words, that he knows the whole to be idolaters. Keil and Delitzsch make the word now decisive, marking the whoredom as lying in fact before them and undeniable, and explain that works are merely an emanation of the state of the heart, in which the demon of whoredom has its seat.
4:
The clause about framing their doings is disputed as much in grammar as in sense. Ellicott notes the margin, that their deeds will not suffer them, which requires the introduction of a word not in the Hebrew\. Though favoured by the Jewish commentators and by Schmoller among others, he prefers the received rendering. Calvin sets out the same two options at more length and reaches the same conclusion: the first makes their inclinations refuse to allow them to turn, so that they were entirely enslaved by their own diabolical inventions and no longer at liberty to return to the right way, which he calls probable but less suited to the context. Gill divides the sense again, asking whether the doings are evil ones they will not leave, as the Targum and Jarchi take it, or good ones they will not choose to do, which are the leading steps to repentance; either way their wills were depraved and had no will to that which is good. Clarke puts it in a line, that they never purpose to turn, having fully imbibed the spirit of idolatry. Calvin alone hears in the verse a declaration that it was all over with the people, incurable and sunk as into a deep gulf with an obstinacy like the abyss; if the prophet speaks in his own person he asks why he wearies himself, having to do with brute animals, or rather with stones than with men. Ellicott lets one sentence stand for the whole, that the knowledge of the only true God is life.

The verb in the verse following divides them the same way. Keil and Delitzsch retain the sense of answering, or bearing witness against a person, as Jerome and others have done, on the ground that the usage is well established and occurs in that sense in Job, and they judge that the reading drawn from the Greek, by which the haughtiness of Israel will be humbled, can hardly be reconciled with the Hebrew phrase that follows. Calvin reports the same alternative, allows that the sense of being humbled is not unsuitable, but embraces the other as most approved: God needed no other witness to convict Israel than their own pride, since a man once hardened thinks there is to be no judgment, his pride taking away every fear. Gill takes it as contradiction and conviction together, the pride of the heart and of the countenance staring a man in the face, so that every action done in a proud and haughty manner flies back at him.

What that pride is remains open. Keil and Delitzsch insist the phrase does not mean the haughtiness of Israel but that of which Israel is proud, or rather the glory of Israel. Ellicott states the same fork plainly, that it may be either the true object of boasting, Jehovah himself, or the false object to which they had yielded, and prefers the latter on the strength of a parallel in Amos. Calvin ties the pride specifically to their contempt of instruction, since they were so swollen with vain confidence that they thought wrong was done them whenever the prophets reproved them, and observes that prosperity had made them insolent, satiety begetting ferocity by the old proverb. Clarke reads it as effrontery in the practice of idolatry, manifesting not only their insolence but the deep depravity of their heart. Ellicott alone draws a historical conclusion from the mention of Judah falling with them: arrogance had led Ephraim on numerous occasions to resent the supremacy of Judah, a jealousy which culminated in the rebellion of the first Jeroboam and characterised their history till the reign of Ahab; and since the involving of Judah is a new note in prophetic utterance, he holds this chapter to have been delivered later than the oracle standing immediately before it.
6:
The failure of sacrifice is agreed and variously explained. Gill will not restrict the going out with flocks and herds to the two tribes, as Kimchi and other Jewish interpreters do, since the ten tribes also, seeing ruin coming, would seek help and pardon by bringing such a multitude of victims as though they had brought all their flocks and herds with them, but without true repentance or faith in the great sacrifice which the legal sacrifices prefigured. Clarke makes the reason their retained spirit of idolatry. Keil and Delitzsch put it as a principle, that God has no pleasure in sacrifices offered in an impenitent state of mind, and read the withdrawal as a refusal to hear their prayers. Ellicott sharpens the point: the spirit in which such offerings are made is of more consequence than the multitude of the oblations, and ghastly and revolting results follow the substitution of ritual of any kind for the weightier matter of the law. Calvin says the prophet laughs to scorn the hypocrisy of a people who thought they had ready at hand a way of dealing with God, and explains what the sacrifices were for: the sinner, reminded by the sight of the victim, should confess himself worthy of eternal death and flee to mercy, looking to Christ, in whom and nowhere else true expiation is found; the faithful never supposed satisfaction to be done by the external work. Wesley reports the tradition of the Jewish doctors that Israel had liberty at this time to bring their sacrifices to Jerusalem.

The treachery is read as marital. Gill compares a woman unfaithful to her husband, since the Lord stood in the relation of a husband to them in covenant. Calvin builds it out of the covenant terms, God binding himself to be Father and Husband and requiring the obedience a son owes and the chastity a wife owes. On the strange children he sets aside two readings: that they had taken wives from heathen nations contrary to the law he calls very frigid, and that they had brought up their children badly, attaching them from infancy to depraved superstitions, he grants is true but insufficient. His own point goes further. Men may abandon themselves to vices for a time and afterwards return to the right way, but when corruption has so prevailed that the children are infected with the same vices, the state of things is past recovery. Ellicott takes the strange children as offspring following in the ways of their mother, with some reference involved to intermarriage with heathen; Wesley has them simply trained up in the same idolatry.

The month is the crux of the last clause, and the voices date it differently. Clarke reads a month of time, within which the king of Assyria would be upon them and oblige them to purchase their lives and liberties by a grievous tax, naming the payment made by Menahem to Pul, and notes that some translate the word not month but locust. Wesley suggests instead the short usurpation of Shallum, which lasted but a month, and takes the portions for all their substance. Ellicott follows Henderson in making the month a personification of the period during which an invasion, closely impending or perhaps already commenced, takes place, and attributes that invasion in part to a king of Judah having sought the aid of Assyria against two neighbouring kings. Keil and Delitzsch pass over the month for the alarm that follows, hearing the horn and the trumpet as the signal by which the invasion of foes was announced to warn the inhabitants, so that the words imply that enemies had invaded the land, and citing Jerome to distinguish the shepherd horn from the trumpet of brass or silver sounded in war or at festivals.
8:
The verse is an alarm, and the voices begin with the instruments. Ellicott distinguishes the two kinds of trumpet named, the cornet made like the bent horn of an animal and the long straight metallic trumpet used for sounding an alarm and convoking the congregation. Gill takes the blast as notice that the enemy is at hand, just ready to invade both kingdoms, and reports the Targum directing the words to the prophets; Wesley addresses them to watchmen. Calvin makes the prophet himself a herald, or one who sends out heralds to proclaim war everywhere throughout the kingdom. That was not properly the office of a prophet, he grants, but he compares the command by which Ezekiel was made to besiege Jerusalem in figure, since after a thousand threatenings the teaching had become frigid and God added visions which more effectually roused torpid men. The truth itself ought to storm not only our ears but our hearts, and be more powerful than any trumpet, yet we see how unconcerned we are.

Where the two places stand is disputed. Clarke makes both of them cities of Judah, in the tribe of Benjamin. Henry sets them in the two kingdoms, a frontier-town of Judah and one of Israel, near together on the confines, so that the warning is sent into both. Ellicott takes them for lofty hills on the northern boundary of Benjamin, and reasons from a parallel in Isaiah that the first lay between Jerusalem and the second, not far from the road which passes northward toward Mount Ephraim; a lofty hill satisfying these conditions was discovered by Robinson, with a prospect over almost the whole tribal region, and with that spot he identifies it. He draws a conclusion the others do not: the prophet does not mention the metropolis, but he reveals the imminent peril of Jerusalem if these high towers, within sight of her defenders, were giving the alarm at the approach of the Assyrian king.

The cry after Benjamin is read two ways. Clarke calls it an abrupt call of warning, the enemy being just behind, and takes the whole for a prediction of the invasion of the Assyrians and the captivity of the ten tribes. Ellicott says the phrase is obscure and translates that the enemy is behind thee, naming Benjamin as the tribe in which the metropolis was situated. Henry has the same sense with the order of judgment spelled out: one tribe is already vanquished, the enemy will be upon the back of the next in a little time, and the cup of trembling shall go round. Wesley takes it otherwise, understanding the words to mean after thy cries, so that Benjamin is called to cry aloud as well, since they too shall fall for their sin.

Henry alone marks the change of figure. The controversy had earlier been described as a trial at law and is here described as a trial by battle, and when God judges he will overcome, so that all should prepare to meet him; what had been spoken of as certain is now spoken of as near, and judgments apprehended as just at the door are very startling and awakening. He adds that the destruction of impenitent sinners shall surely be, not mere talk to frighten them but an irrevocable sentence, and counts it a mercy that it is made known. Calvin ends in the same place from the other side, against those who object that the prophets preach nothing but words: the reproofs of God are not bugbears, he deals in earnest when he reproves the ungodly, and execution follows what he teaches.
9:
The desolation is read as final. Gill has the country of the ten tribes laid waste, the inhabitants destroyed by sword, famine or pestilence and the rest carried captive by Shalmaneser, and takes the day of rebuke either as the day of chastisement or, with the Targum, as the day when they are rewarded for their sins. Keil and Delitzsch press the permanence: the kingdom will entirely succumb, laid waste not only for a time, and the word describing the threatened punishment is the one used elsewhere of lasting plagues with which God chastises obstinate apostasy. Calvin makes the same point by contrast with ordinary providence. God sometimes spares the ungodly while chastising them, and the moderate punishments he inflicts are in a manner an invitation to repentance; but here he lays aside the paternal corrections already applied in vain, since the people had been often warned in deeds as well as in words and still persisted, so that every hope is cut off.

The declaration that follows is read as settled. Keil and Delitzsch note that the perfect tense represents what is proclaimed as a completed event which will not be altered, and take the preposition as against or over the tribes rather than among them. Clarke turns it on the hearers: they have had sufficient warning, and it is their own fault that they have not taken it. Wesley says only that it was made known openly, and by the prophets.

The princes who remove the bound are variously identified, and the figure variously stretched. Gill notes the practice was contrary to the law and has always been reckoned a heinous sin among all nations, done only in secret by such as have no regard to right and wrong, and reports Kimchi and Ben Melech taking the particle not as a note of similitude but of certainty, so that the princes did remove the bound, either literally, seizing the possessions that lay next their own, or figuratively, breaking through all bounds and limits. Clarke keeps the comparison but makes it as strong: they have leaped over the enclosure of law and scaled all the walls of right, despising and breaking all laws human and divine. Ellicott names a particular king of Judah whose pusillanimity brought untold evil on both kingdoms, and observes that the practice is prohibited in the law and included in the curses of Mount Ebal, which he takes as an indication that this very legislation existed before the time of the prophet; the barrier broken down is that between right and wrong, truth and falsehood, Jehovah and Baalim. Wesley reads the ancient bounds as what prevented the encroaching of covetous men.

Calvin alone makes the boundary political. Nothing in the possessions of men is certain unless the boundaries of fields be fixed, and by that metaphor the prophet refers to the whole political order, so that all things were now in disorder and confusion because the leaders who ought to have ruled the people and kept them in obedience had destroyed the whole order of things. He adds a second sense: the tribe of Judah had hitherto been kept separate as by limits, being the heritage of God after Israel was alienated by the defection of Jeroboam, and now the Jews had mixed with the Israelites and become alienated themselves, the princes having taken away the boundaries by destroying all reverence for God and all care for religion. The wrath poured out like water he takes to mean that God would deal much more severely with the leaders than with the common people, while Wesley makes it simply an overflowing flood.
11:
The oppression is traced to different agents. Gill offers three: their own judgments, as the Targum has it, meaning the tyranny of their kings and the injustice of judges who looked only for the mammon of unrighteousness; or the judgment of their enemies the Assyrians, with the taxes laid on them and the devastations made among them; or the judgments of God, since all the enemy did was by his permission and according to his will. Wesley has the ten tribes already eaten up by seditions, civil wars, unjust sentences and bloody conspiracies. Ellicott judges the received rendering probably right, the phrase having reference to rights pertaining to individuals.

The rare word rendered commandment is the crux. Ellicott reports that it occurs in only one other place; that Ewald takes it to mean a wooden post, that is, their idol, which he calls etymologically ingenious but without basis in usage; and that the majority of Jewish and modern commentators take it as the evil ordinance of Jeroboam, who demanded reverence for the calf-symbol of Jehovah. He adds that the Greek translators read a different word and rendered it vanities, followed by the Targum and the Syriac, and thinks this worthy of attention. Clarke and Wesley take the ordinance sense without hesitation, naming the command to worship the calves at Dan and Bethel and to forbear going to the temple, and Clarke makes the point of the verse that many were not forced to do it and did it willingly. Calvin builds his whole comment on that word. The people might have seemed excusable, since religion had not been changed by their voice or by public consent but by the tyrannical will of the king alone, and Jeroboam was moved not by superstition but by subtle wickedness to erect altars away from Jerusalem; yet all were implicated in the same guilt, because the people adopted with alacrity the impious forms of worship commanded. They could not object that this was the act of one man who never consulted them, for their promptitude proved them perfidious.

The moth and the rottenness are read as slowness. Gill has the moth eating garments, penetrating them, feeding privately and without noise, consuming gradually and at last utterly, and reads in it the succession of reigns which secretly weakened the ten tribes before their consumption under Hoshea by Shalmaneser. Wesley makes the comparison briefly and dates the weakening from the death of Jeroboam. Ellicott prefers rottenness to the marginal worm, taking it for the disease of decay, and says both images express concealed causes of irreparable destruction which come suddenly to view when it is too late. Keil and Delitzsch take the moth as destroying clothes and the worm as injuring both wood and flesh, note that the two are joined elsewhere as things which destroy slowly but surely, and quote Calvin himself for the phrase about the slow judgments of God; they add that God becomes a destructive power through the thorn of conscience, which the preaching of the law sharpened. Calvin contrasts the figure with the deluge used before: God compares himself now to little worms that gnaw wood and consume cloths, so that he would by a slow corrosion consume both peoples, sparing them in some measure and yet leaving them unsafe, since they would by little and little feel a decay that would consume them. He adds that the Lord meant in this way to turn the people to repentance, but effected nothing, such was their hardness.
13:
The turn to a foreign power is read as the failure of the chastisement. Gill has the civil state of both kingdoms languid, weak and tottering on the brink of ruin. Clarke says that, feeling their own weakness to resist their enemies, they sought sinful alliances and trusted in their idols instead of calling upon God. Calvin makes the point general: when the Lord deals mildly with us we do not perceive his hand but think that what happens comes by chance, and so seek remedies elsewhere as if we had nothing to do with God. He presses the figure of the patient. The ungodly are blind to the causes of their evils and attend only to present grief, like intemperate men who feel the heat and the pain in the head when disease seizes them, yet have no concern for the disease itself and never inquire how they procured these pains; so the sick man here sighed at the stroke like a brute beast, without judgment to understand whence it came. Keil and Delitzsch read the two attempts at rescue as consequences of the coming of God to punish, and note that the word for the injury means neither a bandage nor a cure but comes from a verb meaning to squeeze out.

The name of the king they sent to is a puzzle. Clarke observes that it occurs nowhere in Scripture but here and in one later place, and reports that the Vulgate and the Targum render it an avenger, a person thought able to save them; he names the alliances of Menahem with Pul and Tiglath-pileser, and of Ahaz for Judah, and concludes that far from healing them the Assyrians made the wound more dangerous by making them tributary. Ellicott gives the word a separate excursus, reporting Schrader that it is not a proper name, since none such is found in the Assyrian lists, but an appellative meaning king Combat or Contention, and that the uncertainty of the chronology makes it hard to determine which monarch is meant. He notes that Schrader elsewhere abandons the identification he first proposed, and prefers the suggestion that the title would admirably apply to Tiglath-pileser, a warrior of great prowess whom Schrader and Rawlinson identify with the Pul of Scripture, so that the verse would refer to the events of the reign of Menahem; he grants that the explanation, probable as it is, remains complicated with questions of chronology. Wesley names the Assyrian and no more.

The lion marks the change of manner. Calvin makes the contrast explicit: God will no longer be a moth and a worm but will come like a lion with open mouth, and asks whether the Assyrian king can hinder him or be superior to him in power. The slow consuming had been meant to leave time for repentance, and since it proved useless, the people deceiving themselves with vain fallacies, God puts on a new form and goes to battle. Gill reads the two beasts as two conquerors, the one devouring Israel and the other breaking the bones of Judah, with the Romans last of all. Clarke renders the first word as a panther or lioness. Ellicott takes the tearing historically, the trans-Jordanic tribes first, then further provinces, and at last the whole population carried away as in the teeth of a beast of prey, and quotes an inscription numbering the captives taken from Samaria, a fate overtaking Jerusalem later at the hands of Babylonia. Keil and Delitzsch note that the word for carrying away denotes the carrying off of booty, and read the withdrawal that follows still from the figure, since as the lion withdraws into its cave so the Lord will withdraw into his own place. Wesley states it plainly, that the divine vengeance by the Assyrians shall be as a lion tearing his prey.
15:
The withdrawal is the last word of the chapter, and it is read as judgment and hope together. Gill takes the going away as a leaving of the countries of Israel and Judah, where God had granted his gracious and spiritual presence to his people, watched over them and bestowed many favours on them, and a going up to heaven, the place of his more glorious presence, as the Targum, Jarchi and Kimchi interpret it; there he shuts himself up, as it were, with respect to these people, as if he had no more thought of them or concern for them. He adds the necessary caution, that this is to be understood in a sense agreeable to the omnipresence of God.

Calvin takes up the same difficulty at length and makes it the point of the verse. The mode of speaking seems apparently strange, since God neither so hides himself in heaven that he neglects human affairs, nor withdraws his hand but that he sustains the world by the continued exercise of his power, nor takes away his Spirit from men, and least of all when he would lead them to repentance, for men never of their own accord turn themselves to God but by his hidden influence. What is meant, therefore, is the external state of the people: after the two kingdoms are cut off God will for a time hide his face from both, and they will think that he cares not for their salvation and that they are far removed from him. These forms of speech, Calvin concludes, are accommodated to the perceptions of men.

Calvin also weighs the last verb. The word properly signifies the morning, so that the verb means to seek early, or to rise early, as men do when they apply themselves diligently to anything; but in many places of Scripture it is taken simply in the sense of seeking, and that simpler meaning he judges most suitable here. The sense he draws is that God, after having been dreadfully fierce against both kingdoms, would for a time rest quietly and wait from heaven to see what they would do, until at length they returned to a sane mind, lost their perverseness, acknowledged their sins and were truly humbled.

The others end on the hope. Clarke makes the abandonment temporary and conditional, lasting till they acknowledge their offences, and observes that it had the wished-for effect, as the chapter following shows, since they repented and turned to God and he had mercy upon them; he adds a judgment on the writing itself, that these two verses are to be considered instances of the true sublime. Ellicott says that tenderness blends with judgment here, and that insulted love bleeds and hopes. He notes that the image of the lion is dropped and that the place spoken of is heaven, and reads the promise through a parable: God will cause all manifestations of his regard for them to cease till they suffer punishment and seek his face, and then, like the prodigal in the flush of a new morning, they will arise and go unto the Father.
